ECE 685 | Power Systems Design L11
Transformer Modeling II
From winding physics to a checked operating-point
model
Buxin She
Mike Wiegers Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering

Lecture outline
1 Build the practical transformer model from physical effects
2 Refer the circuit and justify the input-shunt approximation
3 Solve a complete load example using the chosen circuit model
Voltage and current phasor magnitudes are RMS; referring a phasor across an ideal
transformer does not change that convention.

PART 1
Practical transformer model
Winding effects, core excitation, and the exact equivalent circuit

Ideal-model limitation
STARTING PROBLEM
A loaded transformer has the correct turns
ratio, yet its terminal voltage is below the
ideal value and its input power exceeds its
output power. Which physical effects must a
practical model add?

ECE 685 | Transformer Modeling II 25/32

Limits of the steady-state model
The equivalent circuit assumes sinusoidal steady state and constant parameters near
the operating point.
Saturation: core permeability changes with flux level, so a fixed 𝑋𝑚 is
insufficient.
Inrush: energization can produce a large transient current that a steady-state
phasor circuit cannot predict.
Excitation harmonics: a nonlinear core draws nonsinusoidal current even with
sinusoidal voltage.
Surges: fast transients require winding capacitances absent from this circuit.
Choose a model that includes the physical effect being studied.
Source: Glover et al., 6th ed., Sec. 3.2, pp. 105–107.
